newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN says killings of returnees on rise in Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: UN says killings of returnees on rise in Rwanda.

text.p: The United Nations human rights office on Tuesday reported a marked increase in the number of killings of Rwandan Hutu returnees from east Zaire and Tanzania.

It said in a statement that at least 60 returnees had been killed or attacked in the past two months, including 31 who were beaten to death, killed with machetes or hanged by local people in a single incident in southeastern Rusumo village in January.
Half a million Rwandan Hutus in Tanzania were expelled by troops in December and 600,000 returned home from east Zaire.

The refugees fled their homes in fear of reprisal for 1994's Hutu-led slaughter of minority Tutsis in Rwanda, where genocide wounds are still fresh among survivors who have yet to finish burying their dead in hundreds of mass graves.
The human rights office said that it had also received reports of returnees implicated as perpetrators in a number of killings of genocide survivors and their relatives.

Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army, which swept to power after the genocide, has killed dozens of unarmed peasants in recent weeks during a hunt for Hutu rebels blamed by the government for a new wave of killings since the mass returns.

At least 6,800 returnees were arrested, many by non-competent authorities lacking warrants, the human rights office said. The fresh wave of arrests had exacerbated overcrowding at Rwanda's jails, stuffed with more than 90,000 Hutus accused of genocide.

It said Rwandan government troops or state agents were behind the killing of 13 out of 15 returnees in December in southeastern Kibungo region, which was hard hit by the genocide, including one refugee who was summarily executed in public.
The human rights office said tensions were also increasing amid disputes over housing in Africa's most crowded country.
Many Hutu houses are occupied by ethnic Tutsis, 800,000 of whom returned home from exile after Tutsis swept to power.
